extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of philosophy (early modern/Descartes)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the evaluative principles and methodological maxims René Descartes presents in the Discourse on the Method (his four methodological rules, associated guidance, and his provisional moral maxims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1: Never accept anything as true without clear knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first was never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such; that is to say, carefully to avoid precipitancy and prejudice, and to comprise nothing more in my judgement than what was presented to my mind so clearly and distinctly as to exclude all ground of doubt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid precipitancy and prejudice; include in judgement only what is presented clearly and distinctly enough to exclude doubt. This rule is presented as the foundational screening criterion for beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2: Divide difficulties into as many parts as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: “The second, to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical decomposition: break complex problems into many simple subproblems to facilitate solution. Implicitly recommended as a mechanical step in inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3: Order thoughts from simplest to most complex
rubrics_metrics.description: “The third, to conduct my thoughts in such order that, by commencing with objects the simplest and easiest to know, I might ascend by little and little, and, as it were, step by step, to the knowledge of the more complex; assigning in thought a certain order even to those objects which in their own nature do not stand in a relation of antecedence and sequence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the simplest, easiest-to-know objects and ascend stepwise to complex ones; impose an order of consideration even where natural precedence is absent. This is the methodological rule that prescribes the sequence of reasoning (mathematical-style building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4: Make complete enumerations and general reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: “The last, in every case to make enumerations so complete, and reviews so general, that I might be assured that nothing was omitted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure exhaustiveness by making complete enumerations and broad reviews so as to avoid omissions. Used as a safeguard against overlooked conditions or exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/generalization practice: consider relations in most general form
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes proposes using the mathematicians' success as a model: consider relations or proportions in the most general form possible, not restricted to particular objects, to facilitate application across classes of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational recommendations include: (a) borrow advantages of geometrical analysis and algebra while avoiding their defects; (b) represent relations by straight lines (as simplest objects) to aid imagination; (c) express aggregates with brief characters for memory — all meant to make reasoning clearer, more general, and more applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuild beliefs by systematic doubt (radical reformation of opinions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes resolved to 'sweep [his opinions] wholly away' so as to be in a position to admit others only after scrutiny by reason; he compares the private reformation of one's opinions to rebuilding one's own house after pulling it down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a methodological stance: suspend acceptance of prior beliefs, subject them to examination, and rebuild knowledge on foundations one has personally ensured to be sound. He warns this is not a prescription for everyone but a personal methodological program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on plurality of suffrages as proof of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “I was thus led to infer that the ground of our opinions is far more custom and example than any certain knowledge... a plurality of suffrages is no guarantee of truth where it is at all of difficult discovery, as in such cases it is much more likely that it will be found by one than by many.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using consensus or the number of adherents as evidence of truth in hard-to-discover matters; prioritize individual rigorous demonstration over mere majority opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical appraisal of traditional logic for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes criticizes logic (syllogisms and many precepts) as more useful for communicating what is already known than for discovering the unknown, and notes many precepts are injurious or superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logic selectively: recognize its strengths in exposition and transmission, but seek a method that better supports discovery (hence his preference for a lean set of rules and mathematical-style method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites before undertaking foundational philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: He believed that foundational inquiries in philosophy require preparation: eradicating erroneous opinions, amassing varied experience as material for reasonings, and practising the chosen method to increase skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not precipitately approach the foundations of philosophy; first prepare by removing prejudices, collecting empirical material, and training in the method so one can perform the inquiry with due circumspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experience and varied life situations as material for judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Descartes recounts spending youth travelling, visiting courts and armies, collecting varied experience and reflecting upon it to secure improvement and to find truth in reasonings tied to lived consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather concrete, varied experience and test reasonings against practical consequences; value experiences where error carries immediate personal consequences as more reliable guides than abstract speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about public reform vs. private reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: He warns that while an individual may strip himself of past beliefs and rebuild, it is preposterous for private citizens (not called by birth or fortune) to project major public reforms; sweeping public reform is hazardous and not to be lightly attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish personal methodological reformation (advisable for some) from large-scale institutional reform (dangerous and discouraged unless proper authority and prudence exist). This is a normative warning about scope and prudence in applying radical method to public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional moral maxim 1: obey laws/customs and follow moderate opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first was to obey the laws and customs of my country, adhering firmly to the faith... and regulating my conduct in every other matter according to the most moderate opinions... I chose always the most moderate, as much... these are always the most convenient for practice, and probably the best... I placed in the class of extremes especially all promises by which somewhat of our freedom is abridged...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a temporary code for living while suspending judgement: conform to local customs and the moderate views of the judicious; infer real opinions from practice rather than speech; avoid vows or promises that unduly bind future freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional moral maxim 2: be firm and resolute in action; act on the most probable
rubrics_metrics.description: “My second maxim was to be as firm and resolute in my actions as I was able... since in action it frequently happens that no delay is permissible, it is very certain that, when it is not in our power to determine what is true, we ought to act according to what is most probable... and afterwards consider it, in so far as it relates to practice, as no longer dubious, but manifestly true and certain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When truth cannot be known in time for action, choose a course (preferably the most probable) and act decisively; treat chosen practical commitments as settled for purposes of conduct to avoid paralysis and remorse.
